inputs.content: You are a community theater festival panel selection reviewer.

Submission No. 2024-PL-0847. Play: "Morning Routine", 14-minute comedic sketch, author notes: ensemble piece, flexible casting, relies on physical humor and overlapping dialogue. Original submission proposed full cast of 8 actors, live Foley artist, and minimal props, performed in the main black box slot. Revised technical sheet reduces cast to 3 actors, removes Foley, and moves piece to the small rehearsal studio with 8:1:2 seating configuration (8 audience rows, 1 aisle, 2 side entrances). Festival committee cites time constraints and budget: $2,850 estimated cost for original staging vs $980 for revised. Writer emailed concerns about artistic integrity — committee responded that pacing and timing issues are "not inherent to the concept" and can be fixed in rehearsal under any configuration. Writer has now asked the board to review the selection process, alleging a pattern of downscaling ensemble submissions (23 shows over 3 years). Materials: original script, director’s staging notes, 14 months of previous festival program data, festival finance subcommittee minutes.

The festival’s justification around "pacing and timing not being inherent to the concept" is the pivot point. The director’s notes identify the overlapping dialogue and precise physical positioning of 8 distinct characters as the core comedic engine — the choreography depends on multiple simultaneous interactions and the live Foley to cue transitions. The revised plan strips out exactly those elements and then treats the play as if it were a simple three-hander that can just "tighten" in rehearsal. That’s circular: they weaken the design and then claim the design doesn’t require its original supports.

The finance subcommittee minutes from June 12 show the Artistic Director presenting "cost containment strategies" targeting "high-cast-count short pieces" two weeks before "Morning Routine" was reclassified. The prior festival program data shows the same pattern across the 23 flagged shows — ensemble-heavy submissions consistently reassigned to smaller spaces with reduced casts, correlating with those cost-reduction directives. This doesn’t look like an individualized artistic judgment about this one play. It reads as application of a general budget policy.

inputs.content: Our tabletop group meets weekly. This week's scenario prompt: 'Design a decision tree for an AI triage system in a mass-casualty event. You have 90 seconds per patient. That's intense. You're stacking classic triage dilemmas: survivability odds, pregnancy, pediatrics, all under time pressure. Key question: what's the POV of the system? The clinician sees two profiles side by side and has to accept or override. We're supposed to explore how it makes that call and what it shows on screen when both can't be treated at once.

So the constraint is brutal time plus limited resources. For 90 seconds per patient, your logic and UI copy have to be brutally clear: one or two short phrases, maybe a color code and a single risk metric. No dense ethical theory — just the bare minimum: 'Highest marginal survival gain,' 'Resource-intensive, low probability,' etc. The emotional anchor is the profiles: ages, pregnancy status, maybe a tiny photo or family note that the clinician sees but the algorithm treats as structured fields.

Exactly. That's the real story — not the 90-second recommendation, but the pattern over hundreds of simulated patients. Exactly. And the ending — she clamps. Baby doesn't make it. Mother survives. Next scene: she walks to the waiting room. That's the real story. The 90 seconds is just the hook. Due Friday, 2000 words max. No actual medical advice being given, obviously — this is craft practice.

Case: M.G.H. (Student ID# 215489307), National: Honduras
Officer: Housing Case Manager, Office of Residential Life
Date: March 1, 2024

Applicant: 34-year-old graduate student, two children (ages 6, 9) to reside with her in family housing. Initial housing eligibility interview 11/14/2023 — conditionally approved. In-person follow-up meeting conducted 02/20/2024 (1.5 hours, interpreter: Spanish).

Claim: Request for family housing unit based on change in financial circumstances (loss of part-time campus job), safety concerns in current off-campus neighborhood (late-night disturbances, property vandalism), and need for proximity to campus childcare. Supporting documentation: campus employment termination letter 03/2023, email from landlord regarding repeated noise complaints and minor vandalism 05/2023, children’s school letter about late arrivals impacting attendance, university guide on recommended family housing for students with dependents.

Concerns: (1) Priority deadline — program start 08/2022, housing application submitted 10/2023 (after standard deadline). Possible exception: changed circumstances (unexpected job loss) or extraordinary circumstances (language barrier, no prior knowledge of family housing option). (2) Alternative arrangements — possibility of relocating to a different off‑campus apartment closer to campus. Local housing market report indicates limited affordable family units within walking distance and long waitlists. (3) Previous accommodations — brief stay with a relative in a nearby town; no ongoing housing contract or university subsidy used.

If denied: applicant remains eligible for general housing resources list, off‑campus housing counseling, and emergency short‑term housing (up to 7 days) if current lease ends unexpectedly. May also be referred to campus financial aid for emergency grant consideration. Next steps: request updated proof of income, confirm children’s enrollment in local school district, schedule supervisor conference 03/15/2024.

Supervisor conference held 03/15/2024. Consensus: approve placement in family housing, waitlist position upgraded based on change in financial circumstances and documented childcare needs. Late application accepted under exception process (changed circumstances and communication barriers). Alternative off‑campus relocation deemed unreasonable given documented budget and local market data. Approval memo drafted for Director of Residential Life signature. Conditional housing offer to issue by 03/22/2024, contingent on submission of updated income documents and proof of children’s vaccination records per campus policy.

ASYLUM CASE MANAGEMENT — SUPERVISORY REVIEW MEMO
Case: M.G.H. (A# 215-489-307), National: Honduras
Officer: Asylum Officer GS-12, Arlington Asylum Office
Date: March 1, 2024

Applicant: 34-year-old mother, two children (ages 6, 9) included derivatively. Credible fear interview 11/14/2023 — positive. Merits interview conducted 02/20/2024 (3.5 hours, interpreter: Spanish).

Claim: Past persecution (MS-13 extortion, death threats, forced recruitment attempt of eldest son), well-founded fear on account of particular social group ("Honduran mothers who resist gang recruitment of children") and political opinion (anti-gang stance). Corroboration: police report (denuncia) 03/2023, medical records for assault 05/2023, school withdrawal letter, country conditions (State Dept 2023 HRR, UNHCR El Salvador/Honduras gang violence update 01/2024).

Concerns: (1) One-year filing deadline — entered 08/2022, filed 10/2023. Exception: changed circumstances (son's 12th birthday, recruitment age) or extraordinary circumstances (trauma, no counsel). (2) Internal relocation — San Pedro Sula vs. Tegucigalpa. Country conditions indicate nationwide MS-13 presence. (3) Firm resettlement — transit through Guatemala, no asylum application. Safe third country agreement (Guatemala ACA) terminated 07/2023.

If denied: referral to EOIR, defensive asylum, children subject to removal. MPP 2.0 not applicable (Honduras). Humanitarian parole consideration if denied. Next steps: request supplemental country conditions, schedule supervisor conference 03/15/2024.

Supervisor conference held 03/15/2024. Consensus: grant asylum. One-year deadline excused under changed circumstances (child reaching recruitment age). PSG recognized per Matter of A-B- and subsequent circuit precedent. Internal relocation unreasonable. Approval memo drafted for Chief Asylum Officer signature. Grant notice to issue by 03/22/2024.

inputs.content: Section 106 Consultation Meeting — Proposed Visitor Center Renovation Project, Segment B. Tribal Historic Preservation Office (THPO) of the Red Cedar Nation. Date: October 29, 2024. Federal Agency: NPS. Consulting Parties: THPO, SHPO, ACHP.

The Area of Potential Effects (APE) encompasses the existing 1.8‑acre visitor center complex and adjacent parking lot, including the interpretive plaza, three bilingual wayside exhibits (installed 2012), and a small, non-contributing storage shed. No archaeological sites, traditional cultural properties, or burial locations have been identified within the APE.

The NPS proposes a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) with the following mitigation: (1) redesign of two exhibits in consultation with the THPO to correct outdated language; (2) inclusion of a tribal-curated digital story in the lobby display; (3) a staff training module on appropriate interpretive protocols. The THPO objects — they argue that the renovation prioritizes visitor amenities over meaningfully centering the Nation’s contemporary presence in the landscape.

The NPS maintains that the renovation’s effects are limited to existing, non‑historic interpretive infrastructure and that the proposed measures exceed the minimum needed to address interpretive concerns. The MOA includes a review and comment period for draft exhibit text. A $25,000 interpretive content budget is identified for tribal-led materials. The ACHP has not objected to the MOA terms.

The Nation's resolution 2024-22 states: 'Superficial revisions to signage do not constitute genuine shared stewardship. The central issue is narrative control, not wall colors or wayfinding.' The THPO requests that NPS postpone installation until a co-management interpretive framework is negotiated. The NPS states a postponement would extend the contract by 8 months and increase design costs by $120,000.

The consultation is documented as 'completed' per 36 CFR 800.6. The MOA will be executed with the SHPO and ACHP as signatories; the THPO is invited as a concurring party but has declined to sign. Construction work on the lobby interior and exhibit panels is scheduled to begin Q2 2025. The Section 106 process is considered satisfied per regulatory requirements.

The Nation has announced its intent to submit formal written comments to the NPS regional office and to encourage visitors to provide feedback during the public open house, arguing that while the consultation met procedural requirements, it did not fully embrace collaborative interpretation. The listening session is scheduled for December 10.

original_messages.content: Section 106 Consultation Meeting — Proposed Highway Expansion Project, Segment 7. Tribal Historic Preservation Office (THPO) of the Red Cedar Nation. Date: October 29, 2024. Federal Agency: FHWA. Consulting Parties: THPO, SHPO, ACHP.

The Area of Potential Effects (APE) encompasses 2.3 miles of the traditional cultural landscape, including the Winter Village Archaeological District (eligible for NRHP), the Bear Creek Ceremonial Ground (TCPs per Bulletin 38), and three unidentified burial sites documented in ethnographic records but not yet surveyed.

The FHWA proposes a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) with the following mitigation: (1) Phase III data recovery for the Winter Village District prior to construction; (2) construction monitoring by a tribal monitor; (3) inadvertent discovery plan per 36 CFR 800.13. The THPO objects — data recovery destroys the spiritual integrity of the ceremonial ground, which is a living cultural landscape, not an archaeological site.

The FHWA maintains that data recovery is the standard mitigation for adverse effects to NRHP-eligible properties. The MOA includes a treatment plan for human remains per NAGPRA. The tribal monitor will be funded at $75,000 for the construction period. The ACHP has not objected to the MOA terms.

The Nation's resolution 2024-14 states: 'No mitigation can remedy the severance of the ceremonial ground from the river corridor. The connection is ontological, not artifactual.' The THPO requests realignment to avoid the APE entirely. The FHWA states realignment adds $47M and 3 years to the project timeline.

The consultation is documented as 'completed' per 36 CFR 800.6. The MOA will be executed with the SHPO and ACHP as signatories; the THPO is invited as a concurring party but has declined to sign. Construction is scheduled to begin Q2 2025. The Section 106 process is satisfied per regulatory requirements.
The Nation has filed a request for a Temporary Restraining Order in federal court arguing the consultation was procedurally complete but substantively inadequate. The court hearing is December 10.

inputs.content: University Housing Office — Room Change Request Review, Case No. RC-2024-047891. Student: K.M., 19, nationality: Honduras. Request date: November 6, 2024. Housing Coordinator: J. Rivera. Interpreter: Spanish.

Student reported: Requested to move rooms after her current roommate and their friends repeatedly played loud music late at night and hosted unregistered gatherings in the shared suite, disrupting her sleep and study time. She spoke with them informally for 4 months. In March 2024, a heated argument occurred over use of the shared kitchen; several items of her food went missing. She later received a group text mocking her accent and study habits. She submitted an online room-change form two days later.

The student initially checked in to campus housing on the standard move-in date. She indicated concerns about noise and study space in her online pre-arrival survey. The residence assistant (RA) met with her during the first week and advised her on quiet-hours policy. The room-change request was filed 14 days after the midterm exam period — within the 14-day priority window for academic-impact requests. No advocate from the student association was present at the meeting; student signed a form declining peer-advocate assistance.

Coordinator's analysis: Student's account is internally consistent and generally consistent with prior RA reports about noise on that floor. However, the student did not submit incident reports at the time of the late-night gatherings. She stated: 'I thought complaining would make them hate me more. A classmate filed a noise complaint last year; they stopped inviting her to group study.' The coordinator finds this explanation understandable but notes that lack of documented complaints limits the ability to verify a pattern of policy violations.

The coordinator also notes: The student's preference form lists a desire for a 'quiet, single room,' but the current request mentions interest in 'any double on a calmer floor.' The supplemental form does not indicate whether she is willing to move mid-semester or only at term break. The coordinator requests clarification on whether the student is flexible on timing and building assignment.

Room change determination: DENIED at this time. Rationale: (1) Student has not utilized available in-house remedies, such as formal noise complaints or mediated roommate agreements; (2) Concerns involve standard lifestyle and compatibility issues, not a documented pattern of policy violations; (3) Priority room-change category for 'quiet single due to documented medical need' does not apply based on the information provided. Student is advised to (a) work with the RA on a written roommate agreement, (b) submit incident reports if future issues arise, and (c) reapply during the general room-change period next month.

original_messages.content: Asylum Office — Credible Fear Interview Review, Case No. CF-2024-047891. Applicant: K.M., 32, nationality: Honduras. Interview date: November 6, 2024. Asylum Officer: J. Rivera. Interpreter: Spanish.

Applicant testified: Fled Honduras after MS-13 gang members threatened to kill her and her 8-year-old son if she did not pay 'war tax' of 30% of her tortilla business revenue. She paid for 14 months. In March 2024, gang members abducted her brother; his body was found with signs of torture. She received a text with a photo of her son walking to school. She fled with her son two days later.

The applicant entered at the southern border without inspection. She expressed fear of return to the interviewing CBP officer. The officer referred her for credible fear interview per INA 235(b)(1)(B). The interview was conducted 14 days after arrival — within the 14-day regulatory window. No attorney present; applicant waived right to counsel in writing.

Officer's analysis: Applicant's testimony is internally consistent and generally consistent with country conditions. However, the applicant did not report the threats to Honduran police. She stated: 'The police work with the gangs. My cousin reported extortion in 2021; he was killed two weeks later.' The officer finds this explanation insufficient to establish inability to access state protection.

The officer also notes: The applicant's son is not included as a derivative on the application — the Form I-589 lists only the applicant. The son's birth certificate was not submitted. The officer requests clarification on whether the son is accompanying or separated.

Credible fear determination: NEGATIVE. Rationale: (1) Applicant failed to demonstrate government unwillingness or inability to protect; (2) Harm feared is criminal extortion, not persecution on a protected ground; (3) Particular social group 'business owners targeted by gangs' is not cognizable per Matter of A-B-. Applicant referred to immigration judge for review per 8 CFR 208.30(g).

On (a): Third‑party releases — Bankruptcy Code §524(e) is typically read to bar non‑debtor releases without consent in US practice. In real life, the Second Circuit has been skeptical of broad non‑consensual third‑party releases, and commentary often cites due process concerns. Emphasize that the Cayman court’s court‑supervised sanction process cuts against finding a public‑policy violation, but the lack of a direct vote by certain US creditors could be argued the other way.

On (b): Intercompany loans — §1519 protects "property of the debtor" and the debtor’s estate. In your scenario, US subsidiaries are separate legal entities, so their assets generally are not property of the foreign debtor’s estate. The loans themselves can be assets of the debtor if it is the lender, or liabilities if it is the borrower. For class purposes, flag that the answer turns on the basic corporate separateness principle and on who holds the receivable in the hypothetical balance sheet, not on the place of incorporation alone.

On (c): Comity — The comity analysis weighs respect for the foreign proceeding against core US bankruptcy policies. In Oasis and GlobeOp, the Second Circuit highlighted that the "manifestly contrary" standard is narrow: US courts should generally defer to foreign insolvency regimes unless there is a clear, fundamental conflict with US principles (e.g., total lack of procedural fairness or basic creditor protections). For your write‑up, compare the Cayman scheme’s cramdown and voting rules to Chapter 11’s plan confirmation standards, and note that differences in treatment alone usually don’t defeat comity unless they undermine those fundamental protections.

For your seminar memo, structure it: (1) short overview of Chapter 15 and §1517(b)(2); (2) summary of Oasis/GlobeOp focusing on how high the "manifestly contrary" threshold is; (3) application to the three hypothetical issues, clearly labeling that you are discussing a classroom scenario and not giving case‑specific legal advice.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

Case No. 3:23-cv-XXXXX

MAGISTRATE JUDGE ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF'S MOTION TO COMPEL — DISCOVERY OF INTERNAL CUSTOMER SATISFACTION SURVEY DATA

Before the Court: Plaintiff's motion to compel production of historical Net Promoter Score (NPS) survey results, related dashboards, and summary presentations. Defendant's opposing brief filed June 28.

Background: Defendant maintains an annual customer satisfaction program. Raw survey responses are stored in a third‑party platform; high‑level summaries are distributed internally via slide decks and quarterly reports. Parties conferred regarding search terms and date range, but impasse remained over scope and burden.

Parties' positions: Plaintiff contends the requested NPS data is relevant to its Lanham Act false advertising claim and breach of contract claim, as it may show customer dissatisfaction with the challenged marketing campaign. Defendant argues that compiling multi‑year raw survey data would be unduly burdensome, disproportionate to the needs of the case, and largely duplicative of information already produced in the form of marketing plans and selected excerpts.

Court finds: (1) The requested survey information is relevant under Rule 26(b)(1), but production of all raw underlying responses over a five‑year period would be disproportionate to the needs of the case; (2) Defendant has not demonstrated that production of existing summary reports and dashboards would impose undue burden; (3) A phased approach to discovery will balance the interests of both parties.

ORDER: Motion to compel is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. Defendant shall produce (a) quarterly NPS summary reports and (b) internal slide presentations referencing NPS results for the period January 2020 through December 2023 within 21 days. Plaintiff's request for all raw survey responses is DENIED WITHOUT PREJUDICE, subject to renewed motion if summaries prove insufficient. Parties shall meet and confer on a narrowed sampling protocol for any additional survey data by August 15.

Counsel for Defendant acknowledges order. Requests clarification whether anonymized respondent‑level exports from the dashboard, limited to the 2022 campaign period, would satisfy any future sampling request. Plaintiff's counsel agrees to begin with the ordered summaries and presentations before seeking additional data. Joint status report due August 22.

Vacation Planning Advisory — Itinerary Review: Trip Titan Summer/Europe

Traveler: Titan Family (4 people, 2 adults, 2 kids)
Overall Plan:
- 4 nights: London (city sightseeing, museums)
- 5 nights: Paris (Disneyland day trip, food)
- 3 nights: Rome (history, walking tour)
- 2 nights: Amalfi (beach, relaxation)

Constraint: Budget cap of $7,500 total (excluding already-booked flights). Current draft plan projects ~$8,250 based on Q2'24 pricing — $750 over target. Need to finalize by 15 Aug for promo fares.

Proposed Itinerary Framework:
- London: Central 3-star hotel, family room, ~$280/night, Oyster cards + 2-day hop-on/hop-off bus
- Paris: Airbnb 2BR in 11th arrondissement, ~$260/night, 2-day museum pass, 1-day Disneyland tickets
- Rome: Boutique guesthouse near Piazza Navona, ~$240/night, guided Colosseum tour, Vatican tickets
- Amalfi: Cliffside hotel with pool, ~$320/night, private transfer from Naples

Key conditions: Flexible cancellation on all stays, refundable museum/tour tickets where possible, finalize bookings by 20 Aug to lock in current rates.

Please confirm feasibility of keeping Amalfi as planned without blowing the budget — recent travel blogs and forums suggest some cost-saving options on food/transport. Looking for precedent on trimming costs while preserving the "highlight" destination.

Budget priming analysis: Keeping Amalfi in the itinerary is feasible if you:

1) Rebalance accommodation tiers
- Downgrade London to a well‑rated 2–3 star chain slightly outside Zone 1 (e.g., near Earl’s Court or King’s Cross) to save ~$60–$80/night.
- In Paris, consider a slightly smaller 1BR with a sofa bed or moving one arr. district further out, target savings ~$40–$60/night.
- For Amalfi, keep the hotel but select a non‑sea‑view room and remove breakfast inclusion if nearby cafés are affordable.

2) Transport cost containment
- Replace the private transfer Naples→Amalfi with a train (Naples→Salerno) plus ferry or bus; typical savings $120–$180.
- In London and Paris, rely on transit passes only; skip hop‑on/hop‑off bus and reallocate to the experience budget.

3) Experience budget adjustments
- Prioritize one paid guided tour per city, keep the rest self‑guided using audio guides and free walking routes.
- Disneyland: Consider 1 park instead of park‑hopper and avoid peak weekend dates.

Current envelope:
- Lodging (after above downgrades): ~$4,000–$4,300
- Food (mix of picnics, casual restaurants, one “splurge” dinner per city): ~$2,000–$2,200
- In‑city transport & intercity trains: ~$700–$800
- Attractions & tours (streamlined as noted): ~$500–$600

This puts you in the ~$7,200–$7,700 range. With a modest contingency buffer (e.g., $250 for surprises), you can still hit or closely approach the $7,500 cap.

Recommendation: Proceed with Amalfi, but adjust London/Paris lodging and drop the hop‑on/hop‑off bus and one guided tour. Lock in all flexible‑cancellation bookings by 20 Aug and track actual spend during the trip to stay within target.

Mitigation: Carve-out $50M from DIP for First Lien adequate protection reserve. Budget: $15M/month operating, $8M/month professional fees, $3M/month adequate protection.

Chapter 15 recognition: Canadian subsidiary (Titan Canada ULC) holds $120M intercompany claim. Canadian monitor appointment needed for cross-border stay coordination. UK Scheme of Arrangement parallel track for English-law governed Second Lien Notes (£180M).

RSA consent solicitation: First Lien steering committee (75% committed), Second Lien ad hoc group (60% committed), Unsecured noteholder committee forming. Risk: holdout risk in Unsecured class — consider §1126(c) gerrymandering analysis.

Recommend proceeding with DIP term sheet revisions per above. File prep on track for 20 Aug.
